q: Which rabies virus component is the main target of virus-neutralising antibodies and the antigen in licensed vaccines?
o: The nucleoprotein (N)
The matrix protein (M)
The surface glycoprotein (G)
e: The G protein forms the surface spikes and induces virus-neutralising antibody.

q: A kennel is contaminated with saliva from a dog later confirmed rabid. Which statement about environmental persistence and disinfection of the virus is correct?
o: It is an enveloped virus that survives poorly outside the host and is inactivated by common disinfectants, including bleach at 1:32 for 10 minutes.
It is a non-enveloped virus that persists for months and needs a stronger regimen than parvovirus.
It needs bleach at 1:10, as for ringworm, because enveloped viruses need higher concentrations.
e: The lipid envelope is readily disrupted, so 1:32 bleach for 10 minutes is effective, as it is for parvovirus.

q: A dog is bitten on the left hind foot by a raccoon. Compared with a dog bitten on the face, this dog is expected to have a longer incubation period. Why?
o: The virus must travel farther by retrograde axoplasmic transport to reach the spinal cord and brain.
The hind limb has fewer blood vessels to carry virus to the central nervous system.
The skin of the hind limb is thicker, which reduces the amount of virus inoculated.
e: Rabies virus travels along peripheral nerves, so the distance from the bite to the brain influences the incubation period.

q: Why does the centrifugal phase of rabies virus spread matter for ante-mortem diagnosis?
o: Virus spreads from the brain to salivary glands and nuchal skin, so RT-PCR on saliva or skin biopsy may detect it.
It produces a viraemic phase in which virus can be isolated from blood.
It causes serology to become positive before clinical signs.
e: After reaching the brain, virus spreads out to peripheral tissues, including salivary glands and hair follicles.

q: Which inclusion body is pathognomonic for rabies encephalitis, and where is it most reliably found?
o: Negri bodies, in hippocampal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells
Bollinger bodies, in epithelial cells of the skin
Cowdry type A bodies, in hepatocytes
e: Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in infected neurons.

q: A stray dog is brought to a shelter with sudden jaw drop, drooling and inability to eat or drink. A technician opens its mouth to look for a foreign body. What is the most important concern?
o: Botulism, for which antitoxin should start immediately
Rabies, because pharyngeal paralysis may be the paralytic form and the technician may have had an unprotected exposure
Aspiration pneumonia secondary to drooling
e: Jaw drop, hypersalivation and dysphagia in a stray animal are a classic presentation of paralytic rabies.

q: A rabies-suspect dog must be euthanised and its brain submitted for direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing. Which method is contraindicated?
o: Gunshot to the head
Intravenous pentobarbital overdose
Inhalant anaesthetic overdose followed by intravenous pentobarbital
e: A gunshot destroys the brainstem, cerebellum and hippocampus, which are the tissues needed for testing.

q: After a bite incident, the 10-day observation period applies to which three domestic species?
o: Dogs, cats and rabbits
Dogs, cats and ferrets
Dogs, ferrets and horses
e: The shedding period before clinical signs is well established only for these three species.

q: A currently vaccinated dog is bitten by a stray cat that tests positive for rabies. According to the NASPHV Compendium, what is the appropriate management of the dog?
o: Strict isolation for 4 months
Immediate revaccination and observation for 45 days
Ten-day home observation with no other action
e: A currently vaccinated animal exposed to a rabid animal is revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days.

q: A bat is found in a room where a child was sleeping alone. The child has no visible bite marks. What is the recommended course of action?
o: Test the bat, and give prophylaxis only if it tests positive.
Observe the child for 10 days before deciding on prophylaxis.
Capture the bat for testing and begin post-exposure prophylaxis unless the bat tests negative.
e: Bat bites can be imperceptible, and a sleeping child cannot reliably report one.

q: Which contact with a rabies-suspect animal does not constitute an exposure needing prophylaxis evaluation?
o: Saliva contacting the conjunctiva during restraint
A bite through thin latex gloves
Handling the animal's fur with intact skin on both hands
e: Exposure needs virus contact with broken skin or mucous membranes. Intact skin contact is not an exposure.

q: An unvaccinated person is bitten by a bat. How is rabies immune globulin (RIG) given?
o: The entire dose is given intramuscularly in the deltoid on day 0.
The dose is given intravenously over 30 minutes on day 0.
As much of the 20 IU/kg dose as possible is infiltrated into and around the wound, and the rest is given intramuscularly at a distant site on day 0.
e: RIG neutralises virus at the inoculation site, so it goes into the wound. The remainder is injected away from the vaccine site.

q: A shelter veterinarian who completed a 3-dose pre-exposure series 3 years ago, with confirmed adequate titres, is bitten by a suspected rabid raccoon. What is the correct post-exposure protocol?
o: The full 4-dose series with RIG
Two doses of vaccine on days 0 and 3, without RIG
RIG only, without further vaccine
e: Previously vaccinated people receive two booster doses and no RIG.

q: Which statement about 1-year and 3-year veterinary rabies vaccines is correct?
o: The 3-year vaccines contain more antigen and give better immunity.
The products are immunologically equivalent, and the difference is the label duration from the challenge studies performed for licensure.
The 1-year vaccines are modified-live and the 3-year vaccines are killed.
e: Duration is a regulatory designation based on the licensure study.

q: Why is a recombinant (canarypox-vectored) rabies vaccine preferred over an adjuvanted killed vaccine in cats?
o: Recombinant vaccines give 5 years of immunity in cats.
Adjuvanted vaccines have a higher (though rare) association with injection-site sarcoma, and recombinant vaccines are non-adjuvanted.
Adjuvanted vaccines are not licensed for cats in the US.
e: Feline injection-site sarcoma is linked to adjuvanted products.

q: Which domestic species is now the most frequently reported rabid domestic animal in the United States?
o: Dogs
Cattle
Cats
e: Cats overtook dogs because dog vaccination programmes have been more successful.

q: A shelter staff member is bitten by an impounded stray dog of unknown vaccination status, and the dog is available for observation. What is the immediate first step?
o: Euthanise the dog and submit the brain for testing.
Begin prophylaxis at once without consulting public health.
Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, then report and seek medical or public health advice.
e: Wound washing greatly reduces virus at the site, and medical and public health consultation determines the need for prophylaxis.

q: How is the NASPHV Compendium of Animal Rabies Prevention and Control best described?
o: A federal regulation that overrides state law
A CDC document that is legally binding on animal control agencies
A nationally recognised reference on vaccination, quarantine and exposure management that is not itself a federal regulation
e: States and localities adopt it through their own laws and regulations.

q: From a One Health perspective, which intervention has been shown to be the most cost-effective for preventing human rabies deaths worldwide?
o: Sustaining at least 70% vaccination coverage in the domestic dog population
Oral vaccination of raccoons and skunks
Expanding human post-exposure prophylaxis access in low-income countries
e: Dogs cause over 99% of human rabies deaths, so vaccinating dogs interrupts transmission.

q: Which pattern is the classic teaching for the clinical forms of rabies in dogs and cats?
o: Dogs more often show the furious form, and cats more often show the paralytic form.
Dogs more often progress to the paralytic form, and cats more often show the furious form.
Only dogs can show the furious form.
e: Either form can occur in either species, but this is the classically taught pattern.

q: How is the direct rapid immunohistochemical test (DRIT) best described?
o: An ante-mortem serum antibody test to confirm vaccination
A screening test performed on saliva or blood
A post-mortem brain tissue test read on a standard light microscope, with performance comparable to DFA in validation studies
e: DRIT is a post-mortem brain test that does not need a fluorescence microscope.

q: A shelter veterinarian must obtain a brain sample from a suspect-rabid animal for testing. What is the key precaution?
o: Freeze the whole head immediately before shipping.
Use a saw while wearing a surgical mask.
Avoid using a saw on the skull, because it can aerosolise infectious material, and submit the refrigerated whole head instead.
e: Sawing bone and brain risks aerosolising virus, and freezing damages diagnostic tissue.

q: Which statement about the age at first rabies vaccination is most accurate?
o: It must be given at exactly 6 months.
It usually starts at about 3 months (12 weeks), and most jurisdictions require it no later than 4 months (16 weeks).
It cannot be given before 6 months anywhere in the US.
e: Label minimums are commonly 12 or 16 weeks.

q: A stray dog has a high rabies antibody titre but no vaccination record. For regulatory purposes, how is the dog classified?
o: Fully vaccinated, because the titre shows protective immunity
Unvaccinated, because a titre is not proof of vaccination status
Vaccinated for travel purposes, but not for quarantine purposes
e: Regulatory decisions need a valid vaccination certificate.

q: A person handles an oral rabies vaccine (ORV) bait without gloves. How does this differ from exposure to an injectable rabies vaccine?
o: Only exposure to the injectable vaccine needs reporting.
Both need identical reporting to public health officials.
ORV bait exposure should be reported, because the bait contains a live-vectored vaccine virus.
e: The baits contain a live-vectored virus, so contact should be reported.

q: A rescue plans to move an unvaccinated dog from a rabies-endemic country into the US. What is required?
o: A same-day USDA health certificate only
A rabies antibody titre result only
A USDA health certificate and an import permit applied for at least 10 days before travel
e: Unvaccinated animals from endemic areas need an import permit in addition to the certificate.

q: What is a shelter's rabies-related public health responsibility at adoption?
o: Tell the adopter the current vaccination status and the legal revaccination timeline, and that a titre cannot replace documented vaccination.
Provide this information only if the adopter asks.
Give a titre result in place of a vaccination certificate.
e: Shelters have a duty to communicate rabies status as part of adoption counselling.

q: In a 2025 prospective study, kittens averaging ~9 weeks old with pre-vaccination rabies titers below the susceptible threshold (<0.1 IU/mL) were given a single rabies vaccine below the standard label age. What happened at the 28-day recheck?
o: None of the kittens mounted a protective titer
Only kittens over 12 weeks responded protectively
All 10 enrolled kittens mounted a protective response (>0.5 IU/mL)
Titers were protective at 28 days but had waned to nonprotective by 12 weeks
e: All 10 kittens, susceptible pre-vaccination with no measurable maternal antibody, mounted a protective antibody response (>0.5 IU/mL) 28 days after a single rabies vaccine given below the standard label age — supporting vaccination at the time of surgical sterilization once MDA has cleared.

q: A rabies vaccination programme in Addis Ababa surveyed 1,057 dog owners. Most were willing to pay, but the median price they would pay was below the actual vaccine cost, and many would not travel to a vaccination point. Which strategy do these findings support?
o: Free or reduced-cost vaccine, with door-to-door delivery for owners who will not travel
Full cost recovery at central points, because most owners were willing to pay
Education campaigns alone, because cost and distance were not reported as barriers
e: 94% of owners were willing to pay, but the median price was less than cost, and 41.5% were unwilling to travel. Free or low-cost vaccine is needed to reach and sustain 70% coverage.

q: A survey of 123 dog-owning households in Mahajanga, Madagascar, found that 84.5% of dogs were owned, most were kept for guarding, 45% could roam freely, and 85.4% of owners knew a dog bite can transmit rabies. Which planning conclusion fits these findings?
o: Owner-targeted vaccination can reach most dogs, but roaming needs to be addressed
Most dogs are ownerless strays, so owner-targeted campaigns would miss most dogs
Owners lack knowledge about bite transmission, so education is the only priority
e: Most dogs had owners, and most owners knew about bite transmission, but almost half of the dogs roamed, which lowers the chance that they are vaccinated and increases contact with people.

q: According to 2021 rabies surveillance in the United States, which statement is correct?
o: Domestic animals accounted for most rabid animals, and dogs were the most common domestic species
Wildlife accounted for about half of rabid animals, and cattle were the most common domestic species
Wildlife accounted for over 90% of rabid animals, and cats were the most commonly reported rabid domestic species, ahead of dogs
e: Of 3,663 rabid animals, 91.5% were wildlife (bats, raccoons, skunks and foxes). Cats (216), cattle (40) and dogs (36) made up 94% of domestic cases.

q: A rescue group plans to import 30 dogs from a country where dog-mediated rabies virus variant is enzootic. Which finding from a CDC-based analysis of imported dogs supports import requirements?
o: The estimated incidence of rabies was about 16 times higher in imported dogs than in the US domestic dog population
The incidence was similar to that of the US domestic dog population
The incidence was lower, because imported dogs need a vaccination certificate
e: An estimated 72,589 dogs were imported each year, and the rabies incidence rate was 16 times higher than domestically acquired rabies in US dogs. The variant has been eliminated from the US since 2007.

q: A survey of 10,664 households in the Philippines used human-to-dog ratios to plan rabies vaccination. Which finding supports using local rather than a single national ratio?
o: Dog numbers were highest in urban areas and lowest in rural areas, so urban targets should be raised
Dogs per 1,000 people varied by setting, being highest in rural areas (256) and lowest on small islands (170)
Dogs per 1,000 people were the same in every setting, so one ratio can be applied nationally
e: Ratios were 256.3 (rural), 213.8 (semi-rural), 208.7 (urban) and 170.0 (small islands) dogs per 1,000 people, so targets and resources were adjusted locally.

q: Rabies control staff in Gujarat, India, want to increase acceptance of mass dog vaccination. Interviews with healers of a temple to Hadkai Mata found that dog vaccination is sometimes seen as interference in how the goddess controls dogs. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Bypass the temples, because faith healing has no role in rabies care
Concentrate on post-exposure prophylaxis campaigns, because beliefs about dogs cannot be changed
Work with healers and temple staff to find common ground and tailor messages to local beliefs
e: Traditional treatment often delayed conventional post-exposure prophylaxis. The authors recommend multidisciplinary approaches that look for mutual understanding and context-tailored, locally acceptable messages.

q: Rabies has no effective therapy, and research into combination treatments is limited by how rarely human cases occur. Which approach does a One Medicine perspective propose?
o: Human clinical trials only, because dog rabies cases are too few to study
Compassionate critical care and investigational treatment of naturally infected dogs, in appropriate circumstances
Immediate euthanasia of every rabid dog, to prevent any further exposure
e: The authors argue that supportive therapy mimicking human critical care in naturally infected dogs could speed development of a treatment, addressing viral propagation, neuronal degeneration, inflammation and systemic compromise.

q: A qualitative study of dog vaccination in Chad grouped the obstacles described by dog owners and veterinary officers. Into which three levels were the barriers grouped?
o: Biological, economic and legislative
Technological, political and environmental
Economic, socio-cultural and institutional
e: Barriers included vaccine and transport cost (economic), beliefs about dog meat and dogs as impure animals (socio-cultural), and the lack of a national control strategy (institutional).

q: Researchers built the STOP-R index to estimate a country's rabies elimination capacity when surveillance is poor. Which set of country-level indicators does it use?
o: Literacy rate, infant mortality, electricity access, political stability and natural hazards
Dog density, human population, vaccine price, healthcare spending and average income
Number of veterinarians, road density, rainfall, urbanisation and vaccine coverage
e: The five indicators with the best explanatory value were literacy rate, infant mortality rate, electricity access, political stability, and presence or severity of natural hazards.

q: A scoping review of 70 studies of dog owners' knowledge, attitudes and practices on rabies found wide variation in vaccination uptake. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Awareness of vaccine benefits correlates strongly with vaccination practice, so early, targeted communication about campaigns is important
Knowledge about transmission and clinical signs is consistently high, so communication is unnecessary
Vaccination uptake was consistently over 90% in the included studies
e: Uptake ranged from under 1% to over 90%, with no study reporting full coverage. Awareness of vaccine benefits correlated with vaccination (r = 0.69).

q: US surveillance data from 2002 to 2022 show that 39 rabid dogs and 30 rabid cats had a history of vaccination, but only 15 were true vaccine failures. What conclusion is supported?
o: Animals with up-to-date vaccination were far less likely to contract rabies, so vaccination is highly protective and lowers costs
Rabies vaccine failures are common, so most rabid dogs and cats have been vaccinated
Vaccination lowered the risk only slightly, so its economic benefit is small
e: Up-to-date dogs and cats were 130.8 and 93.6 times less likely to contract rabies, and vaccination was projected to prevent $166 million in costs over 10 years.

q: Veterinary professionals in Turkana County, Kenya, were surveyed on behalf of their communities. Which finding best fits their responses?
o: Most communities were thought to be highly knowledgeable, with vaccination cost as the only barrier
Less than half of the community was thought to know about rabies or recognise its signs in dogs, and barriers included lack of awareness, information on campaigns and cost
Professions and locations gave very different responses, so their data are not reliable for surveillance
e: Responses did not differ meaningfully by location or profession, which suggests that any of these professionals can provide valid surveillance data.

q: A mass rabies vaccination campaign in Lusaka, Zambia, did not reach 70% coverage. Which explanation and recommendation are supported?
o: Owners refusing vaccination, so mandatory vaccination should be introduced
Low dog density in cities, so campaigns should be moved to rural areas only
Poor pre-campaign sensitisation and distance to central points, and prioritise higher-density free-roaming populations with private veterinarians as partners
e: Dog density increased with human density, and 86% of Zambia's estimated 3.2 million dogs live in rural areas at low density, which makes logistics costly.

q: According to 2023 rabies surveillance in the United States, which statement is correct?
o: Most rabid animals were domestic, and dogs were the most commonly reported
Most rabid animals were wildlife, cats were the most commonly reported rabid domestic animals, and no human rabies cases were reported in the US, Canada or Mexico
Wildlife and domestic animals were about equal, and one human case was reported in the US
e: Of 3,760 rabid animals, 91.8% were wildlife and 8.2% domestic. Cats, bats and raccoons were the most frequently found.
